newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drug chief praises Peru, Panama on drug war.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drug chief praises Peru, Panama on drug war.

text.p: U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey, just returned from visits to Panama and Peru, on Thursday praised the governments of both countries for their efforts to combat drug trafficking and money laundering.

"Presidents (Alberto) Fujimori and (Ernesto Perez) Balladeres are determined that their children are not going to live in a narco-state," the retired Army general told a news conference at Miami International Airport.

McCaffrey praised Panama's government for its efforts to fight money laundering. Top Panamanian government officials had reacted angrily on Wednesday to comments during his visit that Panama was a major centre for money laundering.

"It is extremely impressive what they have done," he said, noting that money laundering occurs in many places, even in U.S. cities. McCaffrey also reiterated his support for a Panamanian plan to turn the United States' Howard Air Force Base in Panama into an international drug fighting centre.

McCaffrey praised Peruvian officials' work with farmers in cocaine-growing areas, noting he had been greeted by friendly crowds in the nation's eastern region during visits to discuss alternative crops to coca.
"This is a remarkable change in climate in an area that two years ago it would have been worth your life to be outside after 5 p.m. if you were a policeman," he said.

McCaffrey said the main routes for drug smuggling into the United States now are sea routes, with the eastern Caribbean and the eastern Pacific the main conduits and many drugs brought by water into Mexico for shipment north.

Miami has seen a sharp increase in cocaine seizures in recent months. A U.S. Customs spokesman said agents seized almost twice as much cocaine in southern Florida in the fiscal year ended on Oct. 1, with 70,036 pounds (31,770 kg) seized versus 38,666 pounds (17,540 kg) a year earlier, possibly because smugglers returned to Florida after increased pressure on the Mexican border.

McCaffrey said he did not view the increase as a sign of Miami's resurgence as a major cocaine transhipment point, attributing the increase instead to an "enormously aggressive stance" by Customs and the Drug Enforcement Agency.
He declined to discuss at any length charges from the campaign of Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole about the inadequacies of Clinton Administration drug policy.
